title: Git — Version Control
griotIntro: In Saint-Louis, every fisherman notes down each trip out to sea in his logbook — you can always look back to see what was done.
Git is that logbook for your code: every commit is a trace, every branch a separate exploration.

explanation.text: Versioning lets you go back in time, work with others without overwriting each other, and know who changed what and why. Click on the lines of the workflow below to understand each command.
explanation.code:
git checkout -b feature/login
git add .
git commit -m "Add the login form"
git push -u origin feature/login
# then, to integrate changes from main:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# if a conflict blocks the rebase:
git rebase --abort

annotations.note: `-b` creates a new branch AND switches to it in a single command. `main` stays untouched in the meantime.
`add` stages the modified files — Git distinguishes "modified" from "ready to commit" so you can choose precisely what goes into each commit.
`commit` records a snapshot of the staged files, with a message explaining the why, not just the what.
`-u` (upstream) links your local branch to the remote branch: the next push/pull on this branch won't need to specify where.
`fetch` downloads the latest remote changes WITHOUT applying them to your code — a safe information update.

`rebase` replays your commits on top of the most recent version of main: a linear history, but it rewrites the hash of your commits. Trap: never rebase a branch already shared with others — it desynchronizes everyone.
`rebase --abort` cancels the ongoing rebase and puts the branch back exactly in its previous state — useful when conflicts get too complex to resolve cleanly.

timeline.label: Create a branch
timeline.description: git checkout -b: you isolate your work from the already-stable code on main.

timeline.label: Commit
timeline.description: git add + git commit: each change is recorded with a clear message.

timeline.label: Push the branch
timeline.description: git push: the branch becomes visible to the rest of the team on the remote repository.

timeline.label: Open a Pull Request
timeline.description: The code is reviewed by a colleague before being integrated.

timeline.label: Merge
timeline.description: Once validated, the branch is merged into main — the cycle starts over.

useCases: A team of 5 developers each working on a different feature via separate branches, later merged through pull requests.
Rolling back to a stable version of the code right before a bug discovered in production (`git revert` or `git checkout` on an older commit).
Comparing two versions of a file to understand exactly what a colleague changed (`git diff`, `git blame`).

relatedTools.name: GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket
relatedTools.description: Platforms that host Git repositories online and add pull requests, CI/CD, and team management — Git is the tool, they are the platforms.

relatedTools.name: GitHub Desktop / GitKraken
relatedTools.description: Graphical interfaces for Git, useful for visualizing history and branches without typing every command.

relatedTools.name: Husky
relatedTools.description: Automatically runs scripts (lint, tests) on every commit or push via Git hooks.

bugHunt.explanation: A `push --force` on `main` rewrites the shared history and can overwrite other developers' work — avoid it on a shared branch (prefer `--force-with-lease` if truly necessary, or avoid the force push altogether).

practice.question: What is the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase`?
options: `merge` creates a merge commit and keeps history as is; `rebase` rewrites history by replaying commits on a new base
They are two strictly identical commands
`rebase` permanently deletes commits

feedback.correct: Exactly — this is a very classic interview question, mastering it is a real plus.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: merge = combines with a merge commit, rebase = rewrites history.

quiz.question: Which command undoes the last commit while keeping the changes in the working directory (not lost)?
options: git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git commit --amend --no-edit

quiz.question: How do you correctly resolve a merge conflict in Git?
options: Edit the files marked `<<<<<<<`, choose/merge the content, then `git add` and `git commit`
Always use `git checkout --theirs` to automatically accept the remote version on all conflicting files
Undo the merge with `git merge --abort`, then just rewrite the commit message

quiz.question: What is the difference between `git pull` and `git fetch`?
options: `fetch` retrieves remote changes without merging them, `pull` does fetch + merge (or rebase) automatically
`pull` only works on the `main` branch, `fetch` works on any branch
`fetch` automatically deletes obsolete local branches

quiz.question: A `feature/payment` branch is already in a pull request, and 3 colleagues have pulled it locally to review it. You want to "clean up" its history before the final merge with `git rebase -i` then `git push --force`. What is the risk?
options: Your colleagues' history will diverge from yours: their next `git pull` will generate conflicts or duplicate commits
No risk: rebase never modifies the identity of commits already pushed
GitHub automatically blocks any `push --force` on a branch linked to a pull request

quiz.question: In an interview, you're asked why your team systematically uses pull requests instead of pushing directly to `main`. Which answer shows the best understanding?
options: It allows review before integration, often triggers automated checks (CI), and keeps a clear record of who validated what
It's a GitHub convention with no real technical benefit, just a habit
It's only there to deliberately slow down junior developers

quiz.question: You run `git cherry-pick abc123` on your current branch. What happens?
options: abc123 is deleted from the history of the original branch
Commit abc123 is replayed (applied) on the current branch, creating a new commit with a different hash
cherry-pick merges all branches containing this commit

quiz.question: What does `git reflog` do, and when is it useful in an interview context?
options: It only displays remote branches
It deletes unpushed commits to clean up the history
It locally logs every movement of HEAD (commits, resets, checkouts...), useful for recovering a "lost" commit after a reset --hard

culture: "Rebase vs merge" is one of the most persistent debates in dev culture: some teams enforce a linear history (systematic rebase), others prefer to preserve the real merge history. Neither is "wrong" — it's a team convention to know and respect.

pionnier.portrait: Finnish-American software engineer, already known for creating the Linux kernel in 1991, he was in 2005 maintaining Linux kernel development with thousands of contributors scattered around the world.
pionnier.contribution: He designed and developed Git in 2005, a distributed version control system that became the de facto standard for source code management in the software industry.
pionnier.problematique: The Linux project had until then used BitKeeper, a proprietary tool, whose vendor withdrew free access to the community in 2005, leaving the kernel maintainers without a version control tool suited to the scale and highly distributed structure of their contributors.
pionnier.solution: In the span of a few weeks, he wrote Git: a decentralized system where every developer holds a complete copy of the history, designed for speed and data integrity (via SHA-1 checksums) rather than a centralized client-server model.
pionnier.resultat: Git is today the most widely used version control tool in the world, underpinning platforms like GitHub and GitLab, and an almost universally required skill in software development.

ambiguite.question: Are git pull and git fetch + git merge the same thing?
ambiguite.reponse: Yes: git pull is a shortcut that does fetch then merge (or rebase depending on config) automatically. The practical difference: fetch alone gives you time to inspect the changes before integrating them, pull does it in one step without that control.

title: Docker & Containerization
griotIntro: A pirogue always carries the same provisions, no matter which port it docks at — it is self-contained.
A Docker container packages your application with everything it needs to run the same way, everywhere.

explanation.text: Docker packages an app and its dependencies into a portable image, run inside an isolated container — this solves the famous "it works on my machine" problem. Click on the lines of the Dockerfile to understand each step.
explanation.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

annotations.note: The starting image: Node.js 22 on an Alpine base (minimalist Linux, lighter image).
Everything that follows runs inside `/app` within the container.
We FIRST copy just the dependency files — not yet all the code.
`npm install` runs before copying the rest of the code: Docker caches this step as long as `package.json` doesn't change, which speeds up subsequent builds.
The rest of the code is copied only now, after the dependencies are installed.
`USER node` switches to a non-root user before launching the app: this reduces the attack surface if the container is ever compromised.
`EXPOSE` documents the port used by the container — it's purely informational, it doesn't expose anything by itself: you need `-p` on `docker run` to actually publish the port.
Command executed when the container starts — not during the image build.

useCases: Deploying a Node.js + PostgreSQL application identically on a developer's machine, in CI, and on a production server (as in this Teranga Code project).
Isolating several projects that use different versions of Node.js or libraries, without conflict on the same machine.
Quickly spinning up a database for local development without installing it directly on your OS (`docker run postgres`).

relatedTools.name: Docker Compose
relatedTools.description: Orchestrates several linked containers (frontend, backend, database) with a single file — used in this project.

relatedTools.name: Kubernetes
relatedTools.description: Orchestrator for managing containers at large scale (load balancing, automatic restart, scaling) — the step after Docker Compose in production.

relatedTools.name: Docker Hub
relatedTools.description: Public registry of ready-to-use Docker images (node, postgres, nginx...) that you can use as a base.

bugHunt.explanation: Copying all the code BEFORE `npm install` breaks Docker's layer cache: the slightest change in a source file (even without touching dependencies) invalidates the `COPY . .` layer, forcing `RUN npm install` to rerun entirely on every build. You should copy `package*.json` and run `npm install` before copying the rest of the code, so Docker reuses the install layer as long as dependencies haven't changed.

practice.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
options: The image is a fixed template; the container is a running instance of that image
They are two words for the same thing
A container can exist without an image

feedback.correct: Exactly — the image is the recipe, the container is the dish being served.
feedback.incorrect: Think of the metaphor: the image is a template, the container is a living instance of that template.

quiz.question: What is a Docker volume used for?
options: Persisting data beyond the lifecycle of a container (e.g. a database)
Speeding up the container's CPU
Encrypting the image

quiz.question: Why use an "alpine" image (like `node:22-alpine`)?
options: It's a minimal Linux image, so lighter and with a reduced attack surface
It's slower than other images
It only works with Python

quiz.question: What does `docker compose up` do?
options: Starts several containers defined in a `docker-compose.yml` file, with their shared network
Deletes all local images
Compiles the source code into a binary

quiz.question: Why avoid running a container as `root` in production?
options: To limit the impact of a potential security vulnerability (principle of least privilege)
Root is required for Docker to work
It has no importance for security

quiz.question: What is the point of a multi-stage build in a Dockerfile?
options: Reduce the size of the final image by keeping only the necessary artifacts (not the build tools)
Automatically create several containers at once
It's a feature that doesn't exist

quiz.question: In a Dockerfile, why does the order of COPY/RUN instructions impact the speed of subsequent builds?
options: The order has strictly no impact on the cache
Docker caches each layer; if an earlier instruction changes, all subsequent layers are invalidated and rebuilt
Docker always executes instructions in a random order on every build

quiz.question: Is a variable defined with `ENV` in a Dockerfile visible in the running container?
options: Yes, it's available both at build time AND at container runtime, unlike `ARG` which only exists during the build
No, ENV is only available during the image build
ENV and ARG are strictly equivalent

culture: "It works on Docker" has become a running joke among devs who lived through the pre-Docker era of "it works on my machine" — Docker doesn't eliminate every environment bug, but it removes an entire class tied to system dependency versions.

pionnier.portrait: French-American entrepreneur, founder and former CEO of dotCloud, a PaaS (Platform-as-a-Service) platform founded in 2010.
pionnier.contribution: He created Docker, publicly unveiled in 2013, which popularized containerization as the standard for packaging and deploying software applications.
pionnier.problematique: dotCloud's teams had to deploy applications written in very varied languages and environments on shared infrastructure, without one team's dependencies interfering with another's — the "it works on my machine" problem, at the scale of an entire platform.
pionnier.solution: He built Docker on top of features already present in the Linux kernel (cgroups, namespaces) to offer a simple interface for packaging an application and its dependencies into a portable image, run in an isolated and reproducible way on any machine.
pionnier.resultat: Docker triggered massive adoption of containers across the industry, paving the way for tools like Kubernetes, and became an almost unavoidable skill in modern software development and deployment.

ambiguite.question: Is a Docker image the same thing as a Docker container?
ambiguite.reponse: No: the image is a fixed template (like a class), the container is a running instance of that image (like an object). You can run several containers from the same image, exactly like you instantiate several objects from the same class.

title: Continuous Integration & Deployment (CI/CD)
griotIntro: On a building site, every brick laid is checked before laying the next one — no waiting until the end to discover a flaw.
CI/CD applies this principle to code: every change is automatically tested and validated, continuously.

explanation.text: Continuous integration (CI) automatically runs tests on every push; continuous deployment (CD) then automates the release to production. Click on the pipeline steps to see their order.
explanation.code:
# Simplified pipeline example (GitHub Actions)
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

annotations.note: This pipeline triggers automatically on every `push` — no need to launch it manually.
Step 1: install dependencies, essential before everything else.
Step 2: check code quality (style, obvious errors) before running the longer tests.
Step 3: run the automated tests — if a test fails, the pipeline stops here and the build/deployment never happens.
Step 4, only if everything before it succeeded: build the application to put it into production.

timeline.label: Push code
timeline.description: A developer pushes a commit to a branch or a pull request.

timeline.label: Lint & tests
timeline.description: The pipeline automatically checks code style and runs the test suite.

timeline.label: Build
timeline.description: The code is compiled/packaged to produce a deployable artifact.

timeline.label: Staging deployment
timeline.description: The artifact is automatically published to a test environment.

timeline.label: Production deployment
timeline.description: After validation, the change is delivered to end users.

useCases: Every pull request automatically triggers tests on GitHub Actions/GitLab CI, blocking the merge if a test fails.
An automatic deployment to a staging server on every merge to the `develop` branch, to validate before going to production.
Automatic publishing of an npm package on a newly tagged version, without manual intervention.

relatedTools.name: GitHub Actions
relatedTools.description: CI/CD pipeline built into GitHub, configured in YAML directly in the repository (`.github/workflows`).

relatedTools.name: GitLab CI / CircleCI / Jenkins
relatedTools.description: Popular alternatives to GitHub Actions, each with its own pipeline syntax.

relatedTools.name: Vercel / Netlify
relatedTools.description: Automatically deploy on every push, with a preview ("preview deploy") for each pull request.

bugHunt.explanation: Without `needs: test` on the `deploy` job, GitHub Actions runs jobs in parallel by default — deployment can therefore start even before the tests finish, or even while they're failing. You need to add `needs: test` to the `deploy` job to force it to wait for the `test` job to succeed before starting.

practice.question: What is the main goal of continuous integration (CI)?
options: Detect errors as early as possible by automatically testing every change
Completely replace developers
Deliberately slow down releases

feedback.correct: Exactly — "fail fast": catching problems early costs far less than discovering them in production.
feedback.incorrect: CI doesn't replace anyone, it exists precisely to give the team fast feedback.

quiz.question: What is the difference between continuous deployment and continuous delivery?
options: Continuous deployment automatically deploys to production; continuous delivery prepares the deployment but keeps a final manual validation
It's the opposite: continuous delivery deploys automatically, continuous deployment keeps a manual validation
Continuous delivery only concerns unit tests

quiz.question: Why run tests automatically on every pull request?
options: To avoid introducing regressions before even merging the code
Because it's legally required
It's pointless if the team is small

quiz.question: What is a "rollback" in a deployment context?
options: Automatically going back to the previous stable version in case of a problem after deployment
Permanently deleting the code
A type of unit test

quiz.question: What is the point of a "blue-green" deployment?
options: Switching traffic to the new version with no service interruption, with a fast rollback possible
Coloring the interface blue and green
Deliberately slowing down the deployment

quiz.question: Why separate environments (dev, staging, production)?
options: To test under close-to-real conditions before impacting end users
It brings no concrete benefit
To pay more for infrastructure for no reason

quiz.question: In a GitHub Actions pipeline, what is `needs: [test]` used for on a `deploy` job?
options: Automatically deletes the `test` job after execution
Duplicates the `test` job inside the `deploy` job
Forces the `deploy` job to wait for the `test` job to succeed before starting, instead of running in parallel

quiz.question: Why use encrypted secrets (e.g. GitHub Secrets) rather than plain-text variables in a versioned CI config file?
options: Encrypted secrets run faster
To avoid exposing sensitive credentials (API keys, passwords) in the repository history, visible to anyone with access to the code
It has no impact, it's purely an aesthetic convention

culture: The acronym CI/CD hides a real cultural nuance in companies: some teams only have continuous integration (automated tests) without ever deploying automatically, others push all the way to full continuous deployment. The level of CI/CD maturity is often a good indicator of a company's engineering culture.

pionnier.portrait: British author and software engineering consultant, an influential figure in the agile movement, associated with the ThoughtWorks consultancy since the late 1990s.
pionnier.contribution: He extensively theorized and popularized the practice of continuous integration through his reference article "Continuous Integration" (published in 2000, regularly updated since), helping make it a standard software development practice.
pionnier.problematique: In many teams at the time, code from several developers was only integrated together rarely and late, which caused complex merge conflicts and bugs discovered too late, often right before a release.
pionnier.solution: He formalized the practice of integrating the whole team's code very frequently (several times a day), with each integration automatically verified by a build and a test suite, in order to detect problems as early as possible.
pionnier.resultat: Continuous integration has become a standard industry practice, underpinning modern CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins...) used by nearly all professional development teams today.

ambiguite.question: What exactly is the difference between Continuous Deployment and Continuous Delivery?
ambiguite.reponse: Both automatically prepare every change for production. The difference: Continuous Delivery stops just before going to production (final human validation), Continuous Deployment goes all the way automatically, without human intervention.

title: Linux & the Command Line
griotIntro: The terminal is like the griot's language: direct, precise, no detours.
Mastering Linux and the command line means speaking directly to the machine, without a graphical intermediary.

explanation.text: Most servers run on Linux — navigating, managing processes and logs from the command line is a basic skill for any engineer. Click on each command to understand what it does.
explanation.code:
ls -la
cd /var/log
grep -i "error" app.log | tail -20
chmod 644 file.txt
ps aux | grep node
kill -9 <PID>
df -h
lsof -i :4000

annotations.note: Lists all files, including hidden ones (`-a`), with details (permissions, size, date) thanks to `-l`.
Moves into the folder where Linux centralizes its log files.
Searches for "error" (case-insensitive with `-i`) in the log file, and only shows the last 20 matching lines.
Grants read+write rights to the owner, read-only to others (`644`) — a classic for a file that shouldn't be executable.
Lists all running processes and filters those containing "node" — useful for finding the PID of a process blocking a port.
`-9` sends a forced termination signal (SIGKILL) — the process doesn't get a chance to shut down cleanly, use as a last resort.
Shows disk space used/available per file system, in human-readable format (`-h`) — the first reflex when a server behaves oddly (full disk).
Directly finds the process occupying a specific port (here 4000) — more targeted than `ps aux | grep`, very useful before a `kill`.

useCases: Connecting via SSH to a production server to check logs and diagnose an incident in real time.
Killing a stuck Node.js process occupying an already-used port (`lsof -i :4000` then `kill -9 <PID>`).
Automating a repetitive task (backup, file cleanup) with a shell script run by a cron job.

relatedTools.name: tmux / screen
relatedTools.description: Let you keep a terminal session active on a remote server even after SSH disconnects.

relatedTools.name: htop
relatedTools.description: Interactive, visual version of `top` for monitoring CPU/memory usage of processes live.

relatedTools.name: Oh My Zsh
relatedTools.description: Widely used Zsh shell framework for customizing and improving day-to-day terminal comfort.

bugHunt.explanation: `chmod -R 777 .` makes ALL files and folders readable, writable, and executable by any user on the system — a common reflex to 'quickly fix' a permission error, but a serious security flaw on a server, especially in production. It's better to identify the right owner with `chown` and grant minimal rights (e.g. 755 for folders, 644 for files).

practice.question: What does the command `chmod 644 file.txt` do?
options: Grants read+write to the owner, read-only to others
Permanently deletes the file
Changes the file's owner

feedback.correct: Exactly — 6 = rw for the owner, 4 = r for the group, 4 = r for others.
feedback.incorrect: chmod manages permissions, not deletion or ownership changes (that's chown).

quiz.question: Which command shows the currently running processes?
options: ps aux
ls -la
mkdir

quiz.question: What is the pipe `|` used for on the command line?
options: Redirecting the output of one command into the input of another command
Deleting a file
Creating a new folder

quiz.question: What does `grep -i "error" app.log` do?
options: Searches for the word "error" in the file, case-insensitively
Deletes all lines containing "error"
Counts the number of lines in the file

quiz.question: Why use environment variables rather than hard-coded values (like passwords)?
options: To separate sensitive configuration from the source code and avoid committing it
It has no practical benefit
Environment variables are slower

quiz.question: Which command lets you watch new lines being added to a log file live?
options: tail -f app.log
head app.log
rm app.log

quiz.question: What is the difference between a "zombie" process and an "orphan" process?
options: A zombie has finished executing but stays in the process table until its parent reads its exit code; an orphan is a process whose parent terminated before it did
They are two different names for exactly the same state
A zombie continuously consumes CPU, an orphan does not

quiz.question: Why is `kill -9` (SIGKILL) discouraged as the first reflex for stopping a process?
options: kill -9 only works on root processes
kill -9 automatically restarts the process after stopping it
It terminates the process immediately without giving it a chance to cleanly close its files/connections; it's better to try `kill` (SIGTERM) first

culture: The Linux command line remains a genuine cultural marker in tech: some web developers almost never touch it thanks to modern graphical interfaces, others (particularly in DevOps/SRE) spend most of their time in it.

pionnier.portrait: A computer science student at the University of Helsinki (Finland) in 1991, then 21 years old, he used Minix, a Unix-like system designed for educational purposes.
pionnier.contribution: He created the Linux kernel, publicly announced on August 25, 1991, which would become the most widely used free kernel in the world, underpinning countless distributions and systems (Android, the majority of web servers, etc.).
pionnier.problematique: Commercial Unix systems at the time were expensive and closed, and Minix, though free for study, remained limited by its educational purpose and its license, with no real possibility of modification or free redistribution at scale.
pionnier.solution: He developed, alone at first and then with growing help from contributors recruited via Usenet, a complete Unix-like kernel released under a free license (GPL), open to contributions from anyone.
pionnier.resultat: Linux is today the kernel behind the majority of web and cloud servers, all Android systems, and a significant part of Internet infrastructure — one of the greatest collaborative open source projects in history.

ambiguite.question: Are sudo and root the same thing?
ambiguite.reponse: root is the system's administrator user, with all rights. sudo ("superuser do") is a command that lets a normal user run a specific action with root's rights, without staying logged in as root permanently — a finer-grained security practice.

title: Dependency & Environment Management
griotIntro: Every market trader keeps a precise ledger of the goods they owe their suppliers, with the exact quantity.
A package manager (npm, pip...) does the same with the libraries your project depends on.

explanation.text: Package managers install and version a project's libraries. Understanding semantic versioning (semver) and the difference between dependencies/devDependencies avoids surprises in production. Click on the lines for details.

annotations.note: `dependencies` = required for the app to run IN PRODUCTION (e.g. Express, the server framework).
`devDependencies` = only useful during development (e.g. nodemon automatically restarts the server) — never installed in production.
The `^` allows minor and patch updates (5.3.0, 5.2.9...) automatically, but blocks a jump to major version 6.0.0 which could break everything (semver).
Without a prefix, the version is pinned exactly — useful for a sensitive dependency where even a minor update is scary, but it also blocks automatic security fixes.
`npm ci` (unlike `npm install`) requires a consistent `package-lock.json` and installs exactly those versions: it's the command to use in a CI/CD pipeline for a reproducible build.

useCases: Keeping an exact Prisma version consistent across all developers on a team thanks to `package-lock.json`, to avoid the "it works on my machine" problem.
Using environment variables (`.env`) to store secrets (JWT_SECRET, DATABASE_URL) separately from the source code, as in this project.
Regularly auditing a project's dependencies (`npm audit`) before a production release to detect known vulnerabilities.

relatedTools.name: npm / pnpm / yarn
relatedTools.description: Three competing package managers for Node.js; pnpm and yarn optimize disk space and install speed compared to npm.

relatedTools.name: Dependabot / Renovate
relatedTools.description: Automatically open pull requests to update vulnerable or outdated dependencies.

relatedTools.name: pip / venv (Python)
relatedTools.description: Python equivalent of npm: `pip` installs packages, `venv` isolates dependencies per project.

bugHunt.explanation: `git add .` stages the `.env` file containing secrets (database password, JWT_SECRET) because it was never excluded via `.gitignore`. Once pushed, these secrets remain visible in the repository's history even if the file is deleted later. You must add `.env` to `.gitignore` before any commit, and immediately rotate any secrets already exposed.

practice.question: In semantic versioning `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, when do you increment `MAJOR`?
options: For a non-backward-compatible change (breaking change)
For every small bug fix
Only once a year

feedback.correct: Exactly — MAJOR breaks compatibility, MINOR adds backward-compatible features, PATCH fixes bugs.
feedback.incorrect: MAJOR is reserved for changes that break compatibility with previous versions.

quiz.question: Why separate `dependencies` and `devDependencies` in `package.json`?
options: To avoid installing development tools (tests, linters...) unnecessarily in production
Purely for the visual organization of the file, with no real impact
devDependencies load faster

quiz.question: What is a `package-lock.json` file (or equivalent) used for?
options: Pinning the exact installed versions to guarantee reproducible builds
Encrypting the dependencies
Completely replacing package.json

quiz.question: Why use a virtual environment in Python (venv)?
options: Isolate a project's dependencies to avoid version conflicts with other projects
Make the code run faster
It's mandatory to use a variable

quiz.question: What does a vulnerability detected by `npm audit` on a transitive dependency mean?
options: A library used indirectly (a dependency of a dependency) contains a known flaw
Your own code necessarily contains a flaw
npm audit can only detect syntax errors

quiz.question: Why avoid committing the `node_modules` folder to Git?
options: It's large and can be regenerated from package.json/package-lock.json
Git doesn't allow tracking folders
It prevents other developers from installing a different version of the dependencies

quiz.question: A dependency is declared as `"lodash": "~4.17.20"` in package.json. What does the `~` (tilde) allow, unlike the `^` (caret)?
options: The tilde and the caret are strictly equivalent in npm
The tilde only allows PATCH updates (4.17.x), while the caret also allows MINOR updates (4.x.x)
The tilde blocks all updates, including security patches

quiz.question: Why is `npm ci` recommended in a CI/CD environment rather than `npm install`?
options: `npm ci` strictly installs the versions pinned in package-lock.json and fails if the lock file and package.json are inconsistent, guaranteeing a reproducible build
`npm ci` is simply a shorter alias for `npm install`
`npm ci` automatically updates all dependencies to their latest major version

culture: "Dependency hell" is a shared cultural experience among all developers who have worked on an old project: dozens of dependencies with incompatible versions, impossible to update without breaking everything.

pionnier.contribution: He formalized and published the Semantic Versioning (SemVer) specification on semver.org starting in 2009-2011, proposing a clear convention for numbering software versions.
pionnier.problematique: Before SemVer, library version numbers followed very different conventions from project to project, making it hard for developers to know whether an update risked breaking their code or not.
pionnier.solution: He proposed the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format with precise rules: increment MAJOR for a non-backward-compatible change, MINOR for a backward-compatible new feature, PATCH for a backward-compatible fix.
pionnier.resultat: SemVer has become the de facto convention adopted by nearly all modern package managers (npm, Cargo, and many others with variants), and operators like `^` and `~` in package.json rely directly on this specification.

ambiguite.question: Is updating a minor dependency always risk-free?
ambiguite.reponse: In theory yes according to semver (a minor update must remain backward-compatible), in practice no: mis-versioning bugs happen. Hence the use of package-lock.json to pin tested versions rather than blindly trusting semver.
